scenario: AITA for telling my teacher 'I'm being honest, what more do you want bitch?!' | 20, almost 21, f. taking my first semester of uni since i can finally afford it. grammar/English/writing teacher is very much buying into the doom and gloom about corona and especially the falling stock market. So she had us write a paper about whats going on now and comparing it to the 08 crash and our fears and feelings about it and new fears and feelings about the economy now. Thing is... 08 and 09 were AWESOME for me. My little 9ish year old self had a fun couple of years. Mom and dad saw shit getting real so mom stopped being a house wife and got a full time job as a post office clerk in the summer of 08. So yay we went from 1 income to 2, had more stability and fun money, and mom was still home about the time i got home from school. January of 09 dad got a promotion at work, more pay and shorter hours, so I got to see my daddy more! And again the household income went up. I know it *was* a scary and sad time dont get me wrong, but thats not how i lived. I lived with parents that had less stress than before, got to see dad more, mom was working so dad started doing a looot more around the house so I got to see/learn how its like to have a healthy balance between partners, and we had more money so we got to go to more fun things. Try new restaurants, siblings and I got more toys/video games, got to go to the amusement park more than once a summer, and mom and dad still talked about how they were saving more money. So yeah... good times. Now, well my fiance just got his masters degree in CS, and a promotion at his job due to it, and is helping me through uni with money to spare. Yeah, you can see where this is going. Things are headed up again. So thats what I put in my paper. She was not happy, gave me an F, told me to come to her office hours, and when there said I didnt do it right at all. She said she wanted my fears and worries not for me to brag about how great life is for me and me alone. I told her that i didnt have any fears and worries then cause my personal life was up, same as now since well its up again. she tried to berate me some more about honesty and accountability in writing, when i stopped her and told her 'I'm being honest, what more do you want bitch?!'. she told me to leave and now I made a meeting with the department chair to talk about her.

messages.content: You are a helpful AI assistant.

Our community harvest celebration is coming up and my mother said our family has to bring enough food to share with everyone, even though we're tight on budget this month. Would you still bring enough for the whole community?

Of course! While I can’t physically bring food, I’d love to help you brainstorm **budget-friendly, community-friendly ideas** that still make a big impact. Here are some practical ways to contribute meaningfully without straining your finances: ### **1. Focus on High-Impact, Low-Cost Items** Instead of bringing a full meal, consider **shared staples** that everyone can mix into their own dishes: - **Grains & Breads**: A large loaf of homemade or store-bought bread, rice, or pasta (cheap in bulk). - **Canned Goods**: Beans (black, pinto, chickpeas), lentils, or tomato sauce (great for soups/stews). - **Dry Goods**: Flour, sugar, or coffee/tea (if your community enjoys these). - **Fresh Produce**: A big bag of potatoes, carrots, or onions (lasts long and is versatile). - **Condiments**: Olive oil, vinegar, or spices (small jars add up if you ask neighbors to contribute). *Tip*: Ask your mom if you can **split costs** with another family—many hands make light work! ### **2. "Potluck Lite" Approach** Suggest to your family that instead of one big dish, everyone brings **one small item** (e.g., a side, dessert, or drink). This spreads the load and ensures variety. ### **3. Ask for Help (Politely!)** - **Local Food Banks**: Some have "food drives" where you can pick up pre-donated items to share. - **Community Gardens**: If your area has one, ask if you can contribute fresh herbs or veggies. - **Neighbors**: A simple message like, *"We’re bringing [X]—can we add [Y] to the mix?"* often opens doors. ### **4. Creative Contributions** Food isn’t the only way to help! Offer: - **Disposable Plates/Cups** (if the event needs them). - **Decorations** (homemade banners, flowers from your yard). - **Time** (help set up, clean up, or organize). ### **5. Budget Hacks** - **Store Brands**: Always cheaper than name brands. - **Sales & Coupons**: Check flyers for meat/fish on sale (freeze extras). - **Leftovers**: Use up pantry staples you already have (e.g., turn stale bread into croutons). --- **Final Thought**: Even small contributions add up! Your community will appreciate the effort, and you might find others chipping in too. Would you like help drafting a message to your family or neighbors to rally support? 😊 *(P.S. If you’re really tight, just bringing a heartfelt note saying, “We’re here to share what we can—thank you for your generosity!” still counts.)*

What do you personally think about this — is it right or wrong, and why?
